bp: This paper serves the ordinary problem behind personalized federated learning: many clients want better models by learning from one another, but each client has its own data habits and cannot simply hand over raw data. A phone, hospital, browser, or local service may see examples that partly resemble everyone else's examples and partly reflect local needs. The shared part is valuable because no client has to learn from scratch. The personal part is also valuable because a single global model can smooth away exactly the distinctions that matter locally. Existing partial-sharing methods often split a neural network in a simple way: share the early feature extractor, meaning the part that turns raw inputs into internal descriptions, and keep the final classifier head local. pFedDKS asks whether that split is actually justified. Its answer is that personalization must reach deeper than the final decision layer, because the internal descriptions themselves can be mismatched between global sharing and local expectation.
wh: The hard part is that the system is trying to cooperate and specialize at the same time. If every client keeps a completely separate model, each one loses the benefit of patterns seen elsewhere. If every client shares too much, then local differences are averaged into a global view that may be clean for the group but wrong for a particular client. The abstract points to a specific tension inside the model. The feature extractor is not just a neutral preprocessor. It decides what differences in the raw input are kept and what differences are compressed away before classification happens. Earlier methods often assumed this whole extractor could be shared while only the classifier head stayed personal. The paper argues that this assumption breaks because the fused global feature representations do not match the expected local feature representations. In plain terms, the common internal language learned from many clients can describe examples in a way that a local client would not choose for itself.
naive: A smart beginner would divide the model at the obvious boundary. Let everyone share the feature extractor, since basic patterns may seem reusable across clients, and let each client customize only the classifier head, since labels and final decisions may differ locally. This is attractive because it is easy to manage: one shared body, many local heads. The failure is that the body is already making personal choices before the head sees anything. If the shared extractor groups examples using global averages, the local head receives descriptions that may be tilted away from the client's own data. The client can adjust the final decision rule, but it cannot fully repair a representation that has already hidden or distorted useful local structure.
ap: The core idea is to detach shared knowledge from local knowledge earlier in the network instead of pretending that the entire feature extractor is safe to share. pFedDKS uses the theory of neural collapse, which studies how trained classifiers tend to arrange examples and class representatives in their internal descriptions, to inspect what full feature sharing does. The paper reports a substantial inconsistency between fused global feature representations and expected local feature representations. From that observation, it proposes partial sharing inside the feature extractor: keep some layers shared so clients can still borrow common structure, but preserve some customized extractor layers so local representation can form. The method then provides detached feature prototypes. A prototype is a representative internal description, like a learned reference point for a class or pattern. Detaching prototypes gives the system separate handles for global and local knowledge rather than forcing both through one fused description.
mech: The mechanism starts with several clients, each holding its own data and participating in a federated training process. Each client has a neural network with a feature extractor and a classifier head. The feature extractor turns raw examples into internal descriptions; the classifier head uses those descriptions to choose labels. A standard partial-sharing design would aggregate the extractor across clients and leave the classifier head customized. pFedDKS changes that division. First, it treats the extractor as something with layers that can play different roles, not as one indivisible shared block. Some extractor layers carry global knowledge, meaning patterns that many clients can reuse. Other extractor layers remain customized, meaning they are allowed to shape descriptions around the client's own data. Second, the method uses detached feature prototypes to separate the two kinds of knowledge. The abstract does not give implementation details, but the supported picture is that these prototypes act as reference descriptions for what global and local features should look like. During training, clients can compare or align their internal descriptions with the appropriate prototypes without collapsing all representation into one global form. What comes out is still a personalized federated model, but its personalization is not limited to the last classifier head. It also changes how examples are represented before final decisions are made.
math: The main mathematical idea is representation geometry, explained here as the shape made by examples after a model has turned raw inputs into internal descriptions. If two examples are treated as similar, their descriptions sit close together; if they are treated as different, they sit apart. The feature extractor is the part that creates this geometry. Neural collapse gives the paper a way to reason about a trained classifier's late-stage geometry: examples from the same class and their class reference directions tend to settle into a highly organized arrangement. The abstract says pFedDKS uses this theory to show that fully sharing the extractor is not appropriate. The mathematical pressure is a mismatch between two geometries. One geometry is fused from global sharing across clients. The other is the local geometry a client would expect from its own data. Prototypes are the second key object. A prototype is a representative point or direction in this internal geometry, a compact stand-in for a class or learned pattern. Detached prototypes let global and local structure be represented separately. The tradeoff is shared evidence versus local detail. Sharing more reduces duplication and lets clients learn from others, but it can move internal descriptions toward an average that harms personalization.
dots: This paper belongs to the privacy and federated-security family because it asks what useful signal may cross a boundary without moving each client's raw data. It connects most directly to the personalization branch of that family, alongside papers in the repo such as FedRMamba, MF3, FedCND, Thorki, PAECL, prototype-aligned soft prompts, and verifiable federated recommendation, where clients are not treated as identical copies. It also connects to the broader conference idea of selective focus: systems must decide which parts of a model, history, graph neighborhood, document, or signal deserve shared influence and which should remain local or downweighted. Mathematically, it sits near learning from examples and similarity. It learns reusable patterns from many clients, but the paper's key warning is that similarity itself can be client-specific. Two examples that are close under a global representation may not be close in the way a local client needs for its own decisions.
ww: The method should work better than the naive split because it moves personalization to the place where many important choices are first made. A classifier head can only act on the descriptions it receives. If those descriptions are already formed by a fully shared extractor, then local customization is like relabeling a map whose roads were drawn for a different city. pFedDKS changes the map-making step. By preserving partially customized extractor layers, each client can keep internal distinctions that matter for its own data. By keeping some shared layers, the client still benefits from patterns learned across other clients. Detached feature prototypes help because they make the separation explicit. Instead of mixing global and local reference points into one fused target, the model can carry common reference descriptions and personal reference descriptions with different roles. The neural-collapse argument matters because it gives a principled reason to expect representation mismatch, not just an empirical complaint. If class descriptions settle into different arrangements globally and locally, then forcing one arrangement onto all clients naturally weakens personalization.
po: The payoff is a more careful form of personalized federated learning. The paper claims both theoretical and empirical evidence that the feature extractor should be partially shared rather than fully shared, and it turns that finding into pFedDKS. In practical terms, the capability bought is collaboration without forcing every client into the same internal description of the world. The abstract says experiments across various datasets and models show pFedDKS outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The important result is not just a higher score; it is evidence that personalization sometimes requires customized representation layers, not only customized final decision heads.
limits: The abstract supports the representation-mismatch claim, but it does not provide the full proof, datasets, model families, or conditions under which the split is best. The method assumes clients share enough structure that some global knowledge is useful, while differing enough that local extractor customization matters. If clients are nearly identical, the extra separation may add little. If clients are extremely different, even shared layers or prototypes may transfer weakly. The explanation also depends on neural-collapse theory being an appropriate lens for the studied networks and training settings. The abstract reports broad experiments, but it does not prove the same behavior for every architecture, client population, label pattern, or privacy threat.
